### Behaviour of the Learned Policies

Returns, turnover, and path-dependent risk measures from the same held-out run
as the tables above show whether the agent behaves economically coherently, and
how the three learners differ once their equity, reward and position paths are
put side by side.

The TD3 agent is evaluated against four benchmark strategies spanning passive exposure, execution-style references, and a stochastic baseline. Section 6.1.8 sets its risk-adjusted performance against each of them.


**Return aggregation for ratio metrics.**
Roughly 80–90\% of consecutive LOB returns are zero. The mid-price does not
move between most order-book events. This causes $\hat{\sigma}$ to collapse
faster than $\bar{r}$, inflating the naive per-tick Sharpe by $\sqrt{N}$
without any real edge. The pipeline therefore compounds per-tick returns into
the coarsest bar size with at least 50 observations before computing the
Sharpe ratio, which is reported as $\mu/\sigma$ on the aggregated series with
no annualization. Total return, max drawdown, win rate, profit factor, and
turnover are computed on the raw per-step series.

The Sortino ratio is not reported. Aggregation leaves roughly 237 bars, and the
learned policies record fewer than three losing bars among them, so the
downside deviation $\sigma_{\text{down}}$ is estimated from one or two
observations and the resulting ratio is numerically meaningless: one run
returned a Sortino below its own Sharpe ratio, which cannot occur for a single
return series. The statistic is well determined only for the random baseline,
which loses on roughly half its bars. That the learned policies almost never
close a four-minute bar at a loss is itself a consequence of the frictionless
execution model rather than a property to be expected of a deployed strategy.

def _prov_note() -> str:
    """Which rollout the figures show, for the Note line beneath them.

    This belongs under the figure rather than inside the caption. Appended to
    the caption it ran the title to three lines and buried the one phrase that
    identifies the figure; requirement 11 wants the caption to name the figure,
    and the thesis already carries qualifying detail in a Note line.
    """
    if not _plot_prov:
        return ""
    syms = ", ".join(_plot_prov.get("symbols") or []) or "the pooled split"
    runs = _plot_prov.get("runs")
    if runs:
        # Comparison export: name the runs and the matching that makes them
        # comparable, since the reader is being invited to read one line
        # against another.
        step = _plot_prov.get("checkpoint_step")
        note = (
            f"{', '.join(runs)} on {syms}, each from its own "
            f"{step:,}-step checkpoint, evaluated over the same "
            f"{_plot_prov['n_obs']:,} test-split steps. Random has no trained "
            "weights. Tables 4 and 5 aggregate six instruments; this is one."
        )
    else:
        note = (
            f"Rollout shown is {syms} from the same {_plot_prov['training_steps']:,}-step "
            f"checkpoint as the results tables, evaluated over "
            f"{_plot_prov['n_obs']:,} test-split steps."
        )
    # The MLflow run id identifies the artifact for anyone re-deriving the
    # figure, but it means nothing to a reader of the submitted document, so it
    # is kept to audit renders (AUDIT_PLOTS=1) alongside the other provenance.
    if _audit and _plot_prov.get("run_id"):
        note += f" Run `{_plot_prov['run_id'][:10]}`."
    return note

def _no_data_msg(kind: str) -> str:
    return f"{kind} plot data not available — re-run evaluation to generate parquet artifacts:"

# Wrapped at the backslash so every line fits the 160 mm text width; the
# command stays runnable as written.
_RERUN_CMD = (
    "uv run python src/cli.py evaluate \\\n"
    "  -c pooled/td3_hft_lob_state_space_pooled_streaming_selected_dsr \\\n"
    "  --output-dir logs/<run> \\\n"
    "  --only metrics --only benchmarks --only plots"
)

### Reading Performance in the Context of State Design
The benchmark comparison places the TD3 agent's held-out behavior in direct
relation to the reference strategies. Several features of the comparison
are worth stating explicitly.

The test window shows very little net directional movement. Averaged across the
six instruments, buy-and-hold returned $-0.18\%$, TWAP and VWAP roughly
$+0.06\%$ and $0.00\%$, and a random-action policy $+0.07\%$. Against these, the
TD3 agent averaged $+305\%$, three to four orders of magnitude above every
passive benchmark in absolute terms. Because the underlying instruments barely
moved over the window, that difference cannot be attributed to directional
exposure: a policy holding any fixed position, long or short, would have earned
approximately what buy-and-hold earned.

The agent's behavioral profile is consistent with this. Exposure is close to
balanced at $49.8\%$ long against $50.2\%$ short, and turnover is $0.45$ per
step, so the return is accumulated across many small two-sided position changes
rather than held through a single directional bet. This is the opposite of the
structural explanation available to a near-static policy: the outperformance is
generated by trading, not by declining to trade.

The trade-level statistics support the same reading. The agent's profit factor
is $3.41$ against buy-and-hold's, TWAP's, and VWAP's, all within a fraction of a
per cent of unity, and its win rate is $20.4\%$ against approximately $10\%$ for
each passive benchmark. The passive profit factors sit right at unity, which is
what a flat market produces mechanically. The agent's does not.

On drawdown, the agent's maximum drawdown of $-0.65\%$ is shallower than
buy-and-hold's $-1.11\%$, though not by the wide margin seen on the individual
instruments: the aggregate is dominated by a single $-3.3\%$ excursion on META,
the instrument with the fewest events, whereas on the other five the agent's
worst loss stays inside $-0.25\%$. Balanced two-sided exposure limits the loss
any single directional move can inflict.

These figures are measured under frictionless mid-price execution and inherit
the Hypothesis 1 caveat in full: the comparison establishes that the policy
extracts a real signal the passive benchmarks do not, not that the resulting
edge survives the cost of trading on it. Section 6.2 shows it does not.

One interpretation of why this particular feature family carries signal is
worth stating, with the caveat that the present evidence cannot test it. The
state is built around displayed queue imbalance and the queue-weighted
midpoint, and Section 5.3.5 finds that the top-of-book imbalance features carry the
strongest marginal association with the next price move of any group in the
state, while the state's other features carry smaller but non-negligible
correlations, roughly $0.02$ to $0.09$. Those are also
the quantities a liquidity provider uses to position quotes. If providers
reprice against displayed imbalance, the next movement in the mid-price is not
purely an exogenous process the agent forecasts; it is in part the outcome of
quoting decisions conditioned on the same information the agent observes. Price
formation would then be partly endogenous to the state representation rather
than independent of it.

This reading cannot be separated from the two mechanisms set out in @sec-ch-literature-review.
The movement may be mechanical, the thinner side of the book being consumed
first, or informational, imbalance revealing the direction of better-informed
order flow [@Cont2014; @GlostenMilgrom1985]. The three are not mutually
exclusive, and distinguishing them would require identifying liquidity
providers within the message stream, which the MBP-10 schema does not support.

The interpretation bears on implementation rather than on magnitude. If these
features approximate the inputs to a quoting rule, then an agent trading on
them reproduces a liquidity provider's signal while expressing it as a
liquidity taker, on the opposite side of the spread from where such a signal is
ordinarily monetised. Section 5.2 describes the position-level abstraction
under which the agent neither posts nor crosses, and Section 6.2 finds the
learned margin small relative to quote-scale movements. Read together, these
locate the binding constraint in the mode of execution rather than in the
quality of the signal.

Taken together, the benchmark comparison establishes that the agent's
outperformance is not a positioning artefact. Win rate ($20.4\%$ against
approximately $10\%$) and profit factor ($3.41$ against $1.00$) both exceed
every passive benchmark by a wide margin, so the return gap reflects the
quality of individual position changes rather than a fortunate net exposure.
The Hypothesis 1 verdict from the benchmark comparison is therefore two-sided.
The agent clears the existence bar: it extracts a signal the passive benchmarks
do not, with better trade-level economics and a shallower maximum drawdown. The
comparison is, however, run under mid-price execution with zero fees. That is not a neutral choice: zero-cost execution is a subsidy
proportional to turnover, so a comparison whose only asymmetry is the spread the
active strategy does not pay favours the higher-turnover reinforcement learning policy
over the near-static passive benchmarks. Any spread-crossing cost both erases the
agent's own frictionless return (Section 6.2) and narrows its measured advantage
over buy-and-hold. The benchmark comparison thus supports the existence half of
Hypothesis 1 (a coherent, risk-controlled policy) but not a claim of
benchmark-dominating or deployable performance. The economic magnitude is
highly sensitive to transaction cost, as
@sec-execution-model-signal-friction and
@sec-h2-transaction-cost-sensitivity show.
